{{Short description|Chinese-born American applied physicist (1934–2022)}}
'''Chung Liang Tang''' ({{zh|t=湯仲良}}; 14 May 1934 – 31 May 2022) was a Chinese-born American applied physicist.

Tang was born in China, and moved to avoid hostilities in the [[Second Sino-Japanese War]] and the [[Chinese Communist Revolution]], making his way to [[San Francisco]] via Taiwan in 1950.<ref name="cornellobit">{{cite news |title=Chung Liang Tang |url=https://ecommons.cornell.edu/bitstream/handle/1813/112677/TANG_Chung_Liang_Memorial_Statement.pdf?sequence=1 |access-date=11 September 2023 |publisher=Cornell University}}</ref> He completed a bachelor's degree from the [[University of Washington]] (1955), a master's of science degree from [[Caltech]] (1956), and a doctorate at [[Harvard University]] (1960),<ref name="cornellobit"/><ref name="as"/><ref name="optica">{{cite news |title=Chung Tang |url=https://www.optica.org/history/biographies/bios/chung_tang/ |access-date=11 September 2023 |publisher=Optica}}</ref> then pursued postdoctoral research at [[RWTH Aachen University]].<ref name="cornellobit"/><ref name="ijobit"/>

Tang worked for [[Raytheon]] from 1960 to 1964,<ref name="as"/><ref name="nae"/> then joined the [[Cornell University]] faculty as an associate professor.<ref name="cornellobit"/> He was promoted to a full professorship in 1968,<ref name="as"/> and subsequently appointed the Spencer T. Olin Professor of Engineering in 1985.<ref name="as"/><ref name="asobit">{{cite news |url=https://newsletter.sinica.edu.tw/en/academician-chung-liang-tang-has-passed-away/ |title=Academician Chung-Liang Tang Has Passed Away |access-date=11 September 2023 |publisher=Academia Sinica |date=30 June 2022}}</ref> Tang retired from Cornell in 2008.<ref name="cornellobit"/><ref name="ijobit"/>

Tang was elected a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] in 1975,<ref name="apsfellow">{{cite news |title=APS fellow archive |url=https://aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=T&year=&unit_id=&institution= |publisher=American Physical Society}}</ref> the [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]] in 1977,<ref name="cornellobit"/> the [[Optical Society of America]] in 1986,<ref name="optica"/> and a member of the [[United States National Academy of Engineering]] and of [[Academia Sinica]] in 1986 and 1994, respectively.<ref name="as">{{cite news |title=Chung-Liang Tang |url=https://academicians.sinica.edu.tw/index.php?r=academician-n%2Fshow&id=199 |access-date=11 September 2023 |publisher=Academia Sinica}}</ref><ref name="nae">{{cite news |title=Dr. Chung L. Tang |url=https://www.nae.edu/27962/Dr-Chung-L-Tang |access-date=11 September 2023 |publisher=United States National Academy of Engineering}}</ref> He was the 1996 recipient of the OSA's [[Charles Hard Townes Award]], recognized "for seminal and pioneering advances in the field of nonlinear optics and laser physics".<ref name="Tang">{{cite journal | title=OSA Names Award Recipients for 1996 | journal=Physics Today | publisher=AIP Publishing | volume=49 | issue=3 | year=1996 | issn=0031-9228 | doi=10.1063/1.2807554 | pages=119| bibcode=1996PhT....49R.119.}}</ref>

Tang was married to Louise, a mathematics instructor at [[Ithaca College]].<ref name="ijobit">{{cite news |title=Chung Liang Tang |url=https://www.ithacajournal.com/obituaries/bps128256 |access-date=11 September 2023 |work=Ithaca Journal}}</ref><ref name="sonmarried">{{cite news |title=Massachusetts Bridal For Tobey J. Nemser |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1987/10/11/style/massachusetts-bridal-for-tobey-j-nemser.html |access-date=11 September 2023 |work=The New York Times |date=11 October 1987}}</ref> He died on 31 May 2022, aged 88.<ref name="cornellobit"/><ref name="ijobit"/><ref name="asobit"/>
